documents.text: CHAPTER 2 ABOUT ORGANIZATION 2.1 About GAIL (India) Limited GAIL (India) Limited is a Maharatna Central Public Sector Undertaking under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Government of India, headquartered in New Delhi. It is India's leading natural gas company, with an integrated presence across the entire natural gas value chain, covering transmission and marketing of natural gas, production and marketing of LPG and other liquid hydrocarbons, LPG transmission, petrochemicals, city gas distribution, and LNG regasification. GAIL operates one of the largest networks of natural gas pipelines in the country, spanning more than thirteen thousand kilometres, along with LPG pipelines covering over two thousand kilometres. ernship was carried out at the GAIL Complex in Vijaipur, located in the Guna district of Madhya Pradesh, roughly one hundred and ninety kilometres from Bhopal and two hundred and sixty kilometres from Indore. The Vijaipur complex grew alongside the historic Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur (HVJ) natural gas pipeline and today houses two Gas Processing Units that extract LPG and other liquid hydrocarbons from natural gas. In recent years the complex has also become a site for GAIL's clean energy initiatives, hosting the country's first ten megawatt green hydrogen electrolyzer, capable of producing hydrogen through electrolysis using renewable power, along with one of the earliest Small Scale LNG skids commissioned in India. Being a facility of this scale and complexity, Vijaipur handles continuous process operations involving pressurized gas, rotating machinery, and electrical systems, all of which carry safety considerations that field staff and safety personnel must track closely. It was within this operational context that the need for a faster, digital hazard reporting workflow was identified, forming the basis for the project undertaken during this internship. 2.2 Work Culture GAIL's work culture at the Vijaipur complex is shaped strongly by the nature of its operations. Safety is treated as a shared responsibility rather than the concern of a single department, and employees across engineering, operations, and administrative functions are expected to be alert to hazards within their area of work. Structured shift patterns are followed in the process areas, supported by defined reporting and escalation procedures for anything from routine maintenance observations to safety critical events. The Chairman and Managing Director is supported by a set of whole time Functional Directors responsible for areas such as Marketing and Business Development, Finance, Human Resources, and Projects, along with government nominee and independent directors on the Board. At the facility level, the Vijaipur complex is headed by a senior Executive Director or Unit Head who reports into the corporate structure and is responsible for the day to day running of the plant. Reporting into this position is a set of departmental heads covering Production and Operations, Mechanical and Electrical Maintenance, Instrumentation, Fire and Safety, Human Resources and Administration, and Information Technology. Each department follows its own internal reporting line, with junior engineers and officers reporting to section heads, who in turn report to the respective department head. This layered structure ensures that a hazard reported from the field passes through a clear, accountable chain, from the reporting employee, to the relevant department, to the safety desk, and, where necessary, up to facility leadership.
